_status: DRAFT, NOT IMPORTED. Third municipal-level slice in the AF branch (G.13). Sitting in src/data/research/ pending Thomas's review.
_note: This slice is a documented NEGATIVE finding rather than a network of dependencies, and is reported honestly as such rather than stretched. Across every document actually opened, Cairo Governorate's fiscal relationship to the center runs top-down: the center (Ministry of Planning, Ministry of Local Development, the national Cabinet, Parliament's Plan and Budget Committee) prepares, allocates and approves; Cairo's own Executive Council/governor prepares proposals and executes. No primary document was found showing Cairo Governorate independently setting a tax, fee, or tariff rate, and no primary document was found linking any Cairo/governorate-level fiscal instrument to CAPMAS's CPI. The one genuine, quotable statutory fiscal link between national instruments and governorate-level money is the Real Estate Tax Law's Article 28, earmarking 25% of tax collected within a governorate's jurisdiction for that governorate -- itself administered 'in a manner regulated by Cabinet decision.' All three reports below are correspondingly isolated (no dependencies drawn among them or to other corpus nodes) -- per this project's V0.12 convention, an isolated node is not an absence of information but the documented statement that nothing published names this level's inputs, which is exactly the Cairo finding.

_open_questions.question: News reporting (Al-Masry Al-Youm, Al-Watan News) confirms a distinct 'General Diwan' operating budget exists for Cairo Governorate (EGP 8bn for FY2026/2027 vs 5.68bn prior year, approved by Parliament's Plan and Budget Committee), with the governor quoted seeking to 'diversify financing sources.' No primary document (the budget text, committee record, or a Cairo Governorate financial statement) was reachable this session to quote directly.

A April 2026 news item indicates a draft new Local Administration Law was under legislative discussion, which could eventually supersede Law 43/1979's budget-preparation/control provisions. The draft text itself could not be fetched (proxy blocked it) -- worth checking again in a future session.

HCWW's own site hosts a page purporting to reproduce the Official Gazette text of a Cabinet decree amending water tariffs, but the content is embedded in a non-extractable interactive document. Existence confirmed, content not verified.

reports.title: Citizen Budget Plan for Cairo Governorate (FY2024/2025)
reports.publisher: Ministry of Planning, Economic Development & International Cooperation (Egypt)
reports.description: A central-government 'citizen budget' document produced by Egypt's national Ministry of Planning, presenting the public investment plan allocated to Cairo Governorate (EGP 100.5 billion, 21% of national public investment, across 1,284 projects) for FY2024/2025. Not a Cairo-authored fiscal document: discloses no locally-raised revenue, no transfer structure, and no CPI/inflation adjustment. One of a nationwide set of governorate-level plans the ministry issues, illustrating that even Cairo's most visible public 'budget' artifact is a central-ministry product describing money allocated TO Cairo, not one Cairo itself raises revenue for or controls.
reports.cadence_note: Published annually per fiscal year as part of the Ministry of Planning's 'Citizen Budget' series covering all governorates, not just Cairo.

reports.title: Local Administration Law No. 43 of 1979 (as amended), and 2014 Constitution Article 178 (local units)
reports.publisher: Arab Republic of Egypt (People's Assembly / Constitution)
reports.description: Egypt's foundational local-government statute structuring how governorates including Cairo are administered. Article 178 of the 2014 Constitution nominally grants local units 'independent financial budgets' funded partly by 'taxes and duties of a local nature,' but Law 43/1979 assigns budget preparation to each governorate's Executive Council (Art. 33) while vesting control and performance evaluation of governorates in the central Cabinet (Art. 133: 'The Cabinet shall take charge of control of the work of the governorates, and evaluate their performance'). No primary evidence was found that Cairo Governorate raises or manages revenue independently of central-government allocation and oversight -- consistent with news evidence that Cairo's own operating budget is approved by Parliament's Plan and Budget Committee, not an elected local body. UPDATE 2026-08-13 (AF/G.18, municipal-tier round): independently re-verified against the statute's own Arabic text (cross-confirmed across two legal-database mirrors, lawyeregypt.net and lawhub.info -- neither a .gov.eg host, flagged as a sourcing caveat). Article 1 confirms sub-governorate units DO have legal personality: "وحدات الحكم المحلى هى المحافظات والمراكز والمدن والأحياء والقرى، ويكون لكل منها الشخصية الاعتبارية" [Local government units are the governorates, markaz, cities, hay/districts, and villages, and each of them shall have legal personality] -- notably 'qism' (police-district unit) is NOT among the named units. But Articles 43 and 51 show this legal personality does not extend to independent budgeting: Art. 43, "ما يخصصه المجلس الشعبى المحلى للمحافظة من موارده لصالح المركز" [what the governorate's Local Popular Council allocates from its resources in favor of the markaz]; Art. 51, "ما يخصصه المجلس الشعبى المحلى للمحافظة لصالح المدينة من الموارد المقررة للمحافظة" [what the governorate's Local Popular Council allocates in favor of the city from resources established for the governorate] -- markaz/city 'resources' are statutorily governorate-ALLOCATED transfers, not autonomous revenue-raising budgets. No 'General Diwan' (الديوان العام) budget mechanism appears anywhere in the law's text as reproduced, despite that term's use in news coverage of Cairo's own operating budget.

reports.title: Real Estate Tax Law No. 196 of 2008 (as amended, incl. 2026 amendments)
reports.publisher: Egyptian Real Estate Tax Authority / Ministry of Finance
reports.description: Egypt's national property-tax law (10% of net annual rental value, less 30-40% deduction for expenses), administered by the Real Estate Tax Authority -- a federal-level input to Cairo's local finances rather than a Cairo-specific document. Article 28 earmarks 25% of tax collected within each governorate's jurisdiction for that governorate (plus a further 25% of the national total for informal-settlements development). Valuations are fixed for a statutory five-year cycle with revaluation increases capped at 30% (residential) / 45% (non-residential) per cycle -- a fixed administrative cap, not a CPI or inflation-indexed adjustment. Exemption thresholds (raised to 100,000 EGP annual rental value per 2026 amendments) change only by discretionary Council of Ministers/Parliament action, with no automatic price-index linkage found in the law's text.

Multiple targeted searches for a Ministry of Local Development or Cairo Governorate document citing CAPMAS CPI for cost projection, revenue forecasting, or budget adjustment returned nothing -- an explicit negative finding, not an oversight.

The law's valuations are fixed for five-year cycles with flat percentage caps (30%/45%), and exemption thresholds move only via discretionary Council of Ministers/Parliament decisions -- not via any CPI or inflation index. A documented absence, not an inference.
